description_paragraphs: (David Kittredge, 2025, United States, 112 min, in English )

In 1973, Warner Brothers released The Exorcist . The film became a critical and cultural phenomenon, nominated for ten Academy Awards, and it became the highest grossing movie in the studio’s history and the third highest grossing film of all time.

Four years later, the studio released a sequel, Exorcist II: The Heretic . Directed by Academy Award® nominee John Boorman ( Deliverance ), the film had the biggest budget in the Warner Brothers’ history and was one of the most highly anticipated movies of all time.
But Exorcist II: The Heretic would be one of the most infamous critical and commercial disasters in Hollywood history.

Through interviews with director Boorman, stars Linda Blair and Louise Fletcher, as well as critics, filmmakers, and many of the original crew, BOORMAN AND THE DEVIL details the towering ambitions of Boorman and his team: shooting African exteriors on Burbank soundstages, teetering skyscraper shots, using old-school in-camera effects such “ghost glass” and matte paintings, and embracing technologies like the brand new Steadicam rig. But disasters befell the production, Boorman almost died from a mystery illness, and the film barely finished to make its release date… only to see a hostile and disastrous reception.

Rather than a standard sequel, Boorman had set out to make a wholly original film, an “answer” to The Exorcist . But after its public failure, the director was forced to reassess not only his approach to filmmaking, but also whether he would ever make another movie.

BOORMAN AND THE DEVIL is a tribute to the amazing ambition of a generation of 1970s filmmakers and the studios who supported them. It marks the first feature documentary from Emmy-nominated filmmaker David Kittredge, who most recently served as lead editor and co-executive producer on Bryan Fuller’s limited series Queer for Fear: The History of Queer Horror .
Synopsis courtesy of The Film Collaborative
Want to see the film that inspired this doc? Make it a double feature with EXORCIST II: THE HERETIC!
(John Boorman, 1977, United States, 118 min, in English )

In this sequel to one of the most horrifying stories ever filmed, it has been four years since young Regan was possessed by a demon. Now as an adolescent, she has been seeing a psychiatrist to help her with the painful memories. But the protégée of the priest who exorcised Regan believes the demon has not finished with her . . . and the priest is right.
Synopsis courtesy of Warner Bros.
Want to get all the juiciest gossip about how this film got made? Make it a double feature with BOORMAN AND THE DEVIL!
(Gregg Araki, 2004, United States, 99 min, in English )

At the age of eight, Kansas youngsters Neil and Brian played on the same little league baseball team. Now, ten years later, the two boys couldn’t be more different. Neil is a charismatic but emotionally aloof male hustler, while Brian is a nervous introvert obsessed with the idea that he has been abducted by a UFO. When the boys’ parallel lives inevitably intersect, the pair unearth dark, repressed secrets on a harrowing and unforgettable journey of self-discovery.
Synopsis courtesy of Strand Releasing

raw.calendar_title: Once Upon a Time In Seattle
description_paragraphs: (Collide-O-Scope, 2026, United States, 85 min, in English)

Comprised of moments from over 40 films shot in Seattle, and a few irresistible facsimiles, Once Upon a Time in Seattle is part love letter, part loony action adventure, and part free-associative meditation on the transience of landscape in a city that has always had a complicated relationship with honoring its past while moving swiftly (recklessly?) into the future.

There is no linear narrative, and dialogue is kept to a minimum. The city itself is both location and protagonist, while the function of the human characters, or perhaps more accurately, ciphers, is that of a vessel to move us through the city and occasionally offer loose context or comic relief. With one exception, no single existing shot or sequence is sustained longer than a minute, with most individual shots lasting less than 20 seconds, and over half clocking in at 5 seconds or less. The result is a deceptively complex amalgamation of wholly unrelated material, and an impressively unique editorial/directorial achievement.

Surprisingly weaving numerous throughlines from the many disparate existing narratives, while leaving much open to the viewer’s interpretation, scene chronology floats between seemingly non sequitur, to surprisingly, quietly poignant, depending on the viewer’s own history with the city. A hyper-local, one-of-a-kind film experience and an opportunity to examine Seattle’s ever-changing landscape as seen through the camera lens, Once Upon a Time in Seattle offers a unique portal to examine our city’s topography (and vibe!) of the past, both near and distant.

raw.calendar_title: Sleepbomb Presents: The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari
description_paragraphs: (Robert Wiene, 1920, Germany, 77 min, Silent with a live score!)

Northwest Film Forum is excited to present a screening of the evergreen classic The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari with a live score from San Francisco’s Sleepbomb. Witness the horrors of Dr. Caligari’s hypnotic murders with a heavy, and just as hypnotic, score that will change how you see the film forever .

Sleepbomb is a San Francisco-based cinematic psychedelic post-rock band focused on full, original scores for genre films including The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari , Nosferatu and Metropolis , George Romero’s 1968 Night of the Living Dead and the epic swords & snakes of John Milius’ 1982 Conan the Barbarian . Be there!

Musically, Sleepbomb ranges from heavy doom riffs to dreamy shoegaze, dark soundscapes punctuated with shimmering guitar and ethereal organ. Originally stylistically close to a chaotic version of Throbbing Gristle vs Black Sabbath, Sleepbomb has been exploring experimental sounds and forms throughout their career, guided by the band’s love of Godspeed You! Black Emperor, Coil, Neurosis, Sunn 0))), Ulver and Swans, among others. Settling on a drone influenced style of psychedelic post-rock as the overarching theme while exploring other genres as appropriate for each film’s particular style, Sleepbomb’s goal is to re-contextualize the experience of these well known films.”

description_paragraphs: (Dave Fleischer, 1930-1936, United States, 76 min, in English)

Max Fleischer’s ‘Betty Boop’ is back on the big screen with a block of newly restored cartoons in 4K resolution! Join us for a look at Betty’s evolution from poodle to human with her friends Grampy and Pudgy plus a special appearance by Cab Calloway. These cartoons always bring a good cheer so bring the entire family to celebrate ‘The Queen of the Animated Screen’.
CARTOONS IN THIS PROGRAM:
Dizzy Dishes (1930, 6min) Betty Boop’s grand debut!
Bimbos Express (1931, 6min) Betty Boop (with dog’s ears!) is moving; Bimbo comes with his moving van and is smitten with her.
Dizzy Red Riding Hood (1931, 6min) Betty Boop goes to Grandma’s through the woods despite wolf warnings; but Bimbo follows and gives the old story a new twist.
Crazy Inventions (1933, 7min) In a circus tent, Betty, Bimbo and Koko demonstrate some gadgets reminiscent of TV ads; an animated sewing machine gets out of hand.

Betty in Blunderland (1934, 7min) Betty falls asleep doing a jigsaw puzzle and finds herself through the looking glass into a modern, urban wonderland. The shrinking potion comes from a “Shrinkola” dispenser. When most of the characters assemble, Betty sings “How Do You Do” to them. But the jabberwock steals Betty away.
No No A Thousand Times No (1935, 7min) Betty Boop and Freddie appear on stage in a melodrama, wherein Betty sings the title song to the villain.
Song A Day (1936, 7min) At Betty Boop’s Animal Hospital, various species have appropriate ailments. Morale becomes a problem; Professor Grampy to the rescue!
A Language All My Own (1935, 6min) Betty Boop takes her stage act on the road, and plays in Japan to great acclaim.
More Pep (1936, 6min) In a return to the Out of the Inkwell format, Betty Boop invents a pep formula to speed up lazy Pudgy, but it escapes into the real world with rapid results.
Old Man of the Mountain (1933, 7min) Betty Boop goes to see the fearsome Old Man of the Mountain for herself; he sings the title song and a duet with Betty.
Poor Cinderella (1934, 11min) In the only Betty Boop color cartoon, Cinderella (Betty) goes to the ball thanks to her fairy godmother. Later, only her foot fits the glass slipper.
(Yasujirō Ozu, 1961, Japan, 103 min, in Japanese with English subtitles)
The Kohayakawa family is thrown into distress when childlike father Manbei takes up with his old mistress, in one of Ozu’s most deftly modulated blendings of comedy and tragedy.
Synopsis courtesy of Janus Films

raw.calendar_title: Three Bewildered People In The Night
description_paragraphs: (Gregg Araki, 1987, United States, 92 min, in English)

Long unseen and hard to find, Gregg Araki’s debut feature film Three Bewildered People In The Night is a stunning example of low/no budget DIY filmmaking at its best. Following a messy and tumultuous love triangle held together by a gay performance artist, his friend, and her boyfriend, Araki (in an early but unmistakably Arakian way) begs the question of where one might find love in the modern world, if that’s even possible.

description_paragraphs: (Jessica Earnshaw, United States, 2025, 92 min, in English)

Thirty years ago, Gail Ritchey, a young woman from a conservative Christian community in rural Ohio, had a stillborn birth alone and left the evidence in the woods. Now a devoted mother of three, her quiet suburban life is shattered when DNA evidence links her to the infamous cold case of “Geauga’s Child,” leading to her arrest for murder.
Facing a possible life sentence, Gail must confront the weight of societal and religious pressures—and her own long-buried shame—to ﬁght for her freedom.
Synopsis courtesy of Fourth Act Film
